title: Bronchiectasis: Confirm the Structure, Then Control Exacerbations
bottomLine: Bronchiectasis is chronic abnormal bronchial dilatation with recurrent infection/inflammation and impaired mucus clearance. Confirm the diagnosis with appropriate chest imaging, identify treatable causes, obtain sputum microbiology when clinically useful, and build airway-clearance plus exacerbation-prevention care rather than repeatedly prescribing empiric antibiotics without a longitudinal plan.
recognize: Chronic productive cough, recurrent lower-respiratory infections, persistent crackles, hemoptysis and repeated imaging abnormalities should raise suspicion.
Exacerbations are suggested by worsening cough, sputum volume/purulence, dyspnea, fatigue or hemoptysis beyond baseline.
differentiate: COPD and asthma can coexist but do not explain focal/recurrent infection patterns by themselves.
Cystic fibrosis, immune deficiency, aspiration, prior severe infection, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis and selected autoimmune disorders can be underlying causes.
assessment: Define baseline sputum burden, exacerbation frequency, hemoptysis, dyspnea, weight/nutrition, smoking/exposure history and prior cultures.
Assess oxygenation and hemodynamics during acute deterioration; quantify bleeding rather than calling every blood-streaked sputum episode 'minor'.
workup: Use high-resolution CT/chest imaging appropriate to confirm structural bronchiectasis and assess distribution.
Obtain sputum culture before antibiotics when feasible in a clinically significant exacerbation and review prior microbiology to guide therapy.
Investigate etiologies selectively according to age, pattern and clinical clues rather than using one universal panel.
management: Teach individualized airway-clearance techniques and optimize hydration, activity and respiratory physiotherapy support.
Treat exacerbations using severity, prior microbiology, local susceptibility and current guidance; reassess response and complications rather than extending antibiotics reflexively.
Refer recurrent exacerbations, chronic Pseudomonas, significant hemoptysis, declining lung function or unclear etiology to respirology.
medicationSafety: Repeated broad-spectrum antibiotics increase C. difficile, drug toxicity and resistance risk; culture history and allergy/renal function matter.
Long-term macrolide or inhaled-antibiotic strategies require specialist selection and monitoring rather than routine primary-care initiation.
redFlags: Recurrent exacerbations despite optimized airway clearance
counselling: Teach airway-clearance adherence, vaccination, smoke avoidance and when worsening sputum, dyspnea, fever or bleeding requires urgent review.
followUp: Track exacerbations, sputum microbiology when indicated, symptoms, nutrition and pulmonary function; revisit underlying-cause evaluation if disease behaves atypically.
examTrap: Treating every chronic productive cough as COPD and repeatedly prescribing antibiotics without confirming bronchiectasis or addressing airway clearance.
oneLinePearl: Bronchiectasis care is structure plus sputum plus airway clearance—not antibiotics alone.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society respiratory practice resources

title: Pulmonary Hypertension: Recognize the Syndrome, Refer the Cause
bottomLine: Pulmonary hypertension is a hemodynamic syndrome with many causes. Suspect it when unexplained exertional dyspnea, syncope, right-heart findings or disproportionate exercise limitation persist; use echocardiography as a probability/structural assessment and refer appropriately because definitive classification and targeted therapy depend on the underlying group and often right-heart catheterization.
recognize: Progressive exertional dyspnea, fatigue, chest discomfort, presyncope/syncope, edema and signs of right-ventricular strain are common clues.
Symptoms may appear late and can be attributed incorrectly to deconditioning, COPD, obesity or anxiety.
differentiate: Left-heart disease, chronic lung disease/hypoxia, chronic thromboembolic disease and pulmonary arterial hypertension require different treatment strategies.
A raised BNP/NT-proBNP or abnormal echo can support right-heart strain but does not classify pulmonary hypertension by itself.
assessment: Assess exertional limitation, syncope, chest pain, edema, oxygenation, JVP, RV heave, murmurs and signs of connective-tissue, thromboembolic, hepatic or congenital disease.
Review pregnancy status and drugs/toxins associated with pulmonary vascular disease.
workup: Obtain ECG, chest imaging, echocardiography and pulmonary/laboratory testing directed at likely causes.
Screen for chronic thromboembolic disease and other reversible causes when the clinical pattern warrants it; definitive hemodynamic classification is specialist-led.
management: Treat contributory hypoxemia, volume overload and underlying heart/lung/thromboembolic disease while arranging specialist evaluation.
Do not start pulmonary-arterial-hypertension-targeted therapy simply because estimated pulmonary pressure is elevated on echocardiography.
medicationSafety: Pulmonary vasodilators can worsen physiology in the wrong pulmonary-hypertension group and require specialist diagnosis/monitoring.
Pregnancy carries major maternal risk in significant pulmonary arterial hypertension and requires urgent specialized planning.
counselling: Explain that pulmonary hypertension is not one disease and that the cause determines treatment; reinforce urgent review for syncope, chest pain or worsening edema/dyspnea.
followUp: Close the loop on respirology/cardiology or pulmonary-hypertension-centre referral and pending etiologic testing.
examTrap: Treating an echocardiographic pressure estimate as a final diagnosis of pulmonary arterial hypertension and starting targeted therapy before classification.
oneLinePearl: Pulmonary hypertension is a syndrome; classify the cause before you target the pulmonary artery.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society and cardiopulmonary referral principles

title: Sarcoidosis: Prove the Pattern and Screen the Organs That Change Risk
bottomLine: Sarcoidosis is a multisystem granulomatous diagnosis built from a compatible clinical/radiographic pattern, exclusion of important alternatives and tissue confirmation when needed. Management depends on organ threat and functional impact—not the chest image alone.
recognize: Bilateral hilar/mediastinal adenopathy, pulmonary infiltrates, cough/dyspnea, erythema nodosum, uveitis and constitutional symptoms are common patterns.
Cardiac, neurologic, ocular or severe hypercalcemic disease can be far more dangerous than pulmonary symptoms.
differentiate: Tuberculosis, fungal disease, lymphoma, occupational/exposure-related granulomatous disease and drug reactions can mimic sarcoidosis.
A classic presentation such as Löfgren syndrome may be managed differently from unexplained adenopathy with systemic red flags.
assessment: Assess respiratory symptoms/function plus eye symptoms, palpitations/syncope, neurologic complaints, skin findings, calcium-related symptoms and medication/exposure history.
Examine for lymphadenopathy, skin lesions, cardiac clues and organ-specific abnormalities.
workup: Use chest imaging and pulmonary function assessment; select tissue sampling when diagnosis remains uncertain or treatment stakes are high.
Screen for organ involvement using history/exam and targeted ECG, eye, calcium/renal/hepatic or neurologic/cardiac evaluation when indicated.
management: Observe selected asymptomatic/stable patients when organ function is preserved.
Use corticosteroid or steroid-sparing therapy when clinically important organ dysfunction or high-risk organ involvement warrants treatment, usually with specialty guidance.
medicationSafety: Before immunosuppression, assess infection risk including tuberculosis/hepatitis according to current CTS/specialty guidance and monitor corticosteroid or steroid-sparing toxicity.
Do not suppress inflammation before excluding a plausible untreated infection.
counselling: Explain that sarcoidosis can affect organs outside the lungs and that new visual, cardiac or neurologic symptoms require prompt reassessment.
followUp: Trend symptoms, pulmonary function and organ-specific disease activity; refer high-risk extrapulmonary disease promptly.
examTrap: Treating hilar adenopathy alone with long-term steroids before excluding infection and deciding whether organ disease actually requires therapy.
oneLinePearl: In sarcoidosis, the dangerous organ—not the prettiest chest image—drives treatment.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society interstitial/granulomatous lung-disease resources

title: Adult Cystic Fibrosis: Multisystem Care Beyond Pulmonary Exacerbations
bottomLine: Adults with cystic fibrosis require specialized multidisciplinary longitudinal care. Primary/NP care should recognize pulmonary exacerbation and treatment toxicity while also addressing CF-related diabetes, pancreatic/nutritional disease, liver/bone health, fertility/pregnancy, mental health and drug interactions—including CFTR modulators.
recognize: Increasing cough/sputum, dyspnea, fatigue, weight loss and declining spirometry can signal pulmonary exacerbation.
Longer survival means adult CF care increasingly includes diabetes, liver disease, osteoporosis, reproductive planning and age-related comorbidity.
differentiate: New respiratory symptoms may reflect exacerbation, viral infection, pneumothorax, hemoptysis or another cause; do not automatically treat every change as routine bacterial infection.
CF-related diabetes and pancreatic insufficiency have disease-specific management considerations.
assessment: Review baseline FEV1, airway-clearance regimen, inhaled/oral therapies, CFTR modulator, microbiology history, nutrition/weight, pancreatic enzymes, diabetes status and transplant history if relevant.
Assess hemoptysis, pleuritic pain, sudden dyspnea, pregnancy plans and medication interactions.
workup: Coordinate sputum microbiology, spirometry and imaging with the CF centre when exacerbation or complication is suspected.
Use CF-specific screening for diabetes, bone, liver and nutritional complications through the specialty care plan.
management: Do not independently overhaul chronic CF regimens without the CF team; coordinate exacerbation treatment with prior microbiology and specialist protocols.
Maintain vaccination, nutrition, mental-health, reproductive and general preventive care alongside CF-specific management.
medicationSafety: CFTR modulators have clinically important interactions and organ-specific monitoring; check the current product monograph and CF-centre plan before adding interacting therapy.
Repeated aminoglycoside or other antimicrobial exposure creates renal/ototoxicity and resistance considerations.
counselling: Reinforce airway-clearance and chronic-therapy adherence without blame, and coordinate pregnancy/fertility and transition issues with the CF centre.
followUp: Keep specialty follow-up closed-loop and integrate primary preventive care with CF-centre monitoring rather than duplicating or contradicting the plan.
examTrap: Treating adult cystic fibrosis as only recurrent lung infection and missing diabetes, nutrition, bone, liver, fertility or CFTR-modulator safety issues.
oneLinePearl: Adult CF is a multisystem chronic disease managed with a CF centre—not just an antibiotic diagnosis.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society cystic-fibrosis clinical education

title: Mechanical Ventilation Basics: Treat the Patient and the Cause, Not the Ventilator Number
bottomLine: Mechanical ventilation supports gas exchange while the underlying disease is treated. The NP must recognize immediately dangerous patient–ventilator problems, understand tidal volume/pressure/PEEP/FiO2 interactions, use lung-protective principles when appropriate, and escalate rather than making isolated ventilator changes without reassessing airway, breathing, circulation and cause.
recognize: Worsening hypoxemia, hypercapnia/acidemia, high airway pressures, low delivered volumes or patient distress may reflect airway obstruction, secretions, tube displacement, pneumothorax, bronchospasm, pulmonary edema, worsening lung disease or equipment/circuit problems.
A ventilator alarm is a clinical cue, not a diagnosis.
differentiate: High peak pressure with preserved plateau pressure suggests airway/resistance problems; elevated plateau pressure suggests reduced compliance/alveolar pressure burden.
Sudden unilateral breath-sound loss plus shock/hypoxemia raises pneumothorax or tube-position concern.
assessment: Assess the patient first: airway/tube position, chest rise, breath sounds, oxygenation, hemodynamics, mental status/sedation and ventilator waveforms/alarms.
Review mode, set and delivered tidal volume, respiratory rate, PEEP, FiO2 and pressure measurements in context.
workup: Use ABG/VBG when acid-base/ventilation information will change management and obtain chest imaging or bedside diagnostic assessment when tube position, pneumothorax or pulmonary pathology is suspected.
Trend oxygenation, ventilation, pressures and clinical response after interventions.
management: For acute instability, disconnect and manually ventilate with appropriate oxygen if equipment failure or dangerous ventilator interaction is suspected while the airway/circuit problem is assessed.
Use lung-protective ventilation principles in ARDS/at-risk lungs and titrate oxygen/PEEP according to the acute-care protocol and patient physiology.
Escalate difficult synchrony, severe gas-exchange failure, refractory shock or suspected barotrauma to critical-care/RT expertise immediately.
medicationSafety: Sedation/analgesia can cause hypotension/delirium and should support comfort/synchrony without masking deterioration.
Neuromuscular blockade requires deep sedation/analgesia and critical-care monitoring; it is not routine treatment for agitation.
counselling: When communicating with family, explain that the ventilator is support while the underlying illness is treated and that settings change as physiology changes.
followUp: Reassess readiness for sedation reduction/weaning and complication prevention as the acute cause improves.
examTrap: Responding to a high-pressure alarm by changing a ventilator setting before checking the patient, tube, secretions and pneumothorax risk.
oneLinePearl: Ventilator alarm? Patient first, airway/circuit second, settings third.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society home/mechanical ventilation guidance

title: Asthma–COPD Overlap: Treat Asthma Risk While Characterizing Persistent Obstruction
bottomLine: Patients can have features of both asthma and COPD, but 'overlap' is not a reason to abandon diagnostic precision. Confirm variable symptoms and persistent airflow limitation, review smoking/exposures and eosinophilic/allergic features, and when asthma is present ensure an inhaled-corticosteroid-containing strategy rather than bronchodilator-only COPD treatment.
recognize: Asthma clues include variable symptoms, atopy, earlier onset and meaningful bronchodilator variability; COPD clues include persistent symptoms/obstruction with smoking or occupational/biomass exposure and later onset.
Exacerbation history and blood eosinophils may influence anti-inflammatory treatment decisions but do not replace the clinical diagnosis.
differentiate: Do not label any smoker with wheeze as overlap without spirometric confirmation and a credible asthma history.
Heart failure, bronchiectasis, vocal-cord dysfunction and other causes can mimic obstructive symptoms.
assessment: Assess symptom variability, nocturnal/exercise symptoms, exacerbations, allergies, smoking/exposures, inhaler technique/adherence and prior spirometry.
Look for frequent steroid use, pneumonia risk, osteoporosis and other medication comorbidities.
workup: Use spirometry with bronchodilator assessment and repeat/objective testing when the diagnosis remains uncertain.
Evaluate alternative causes or specialist testing when obstruction is disproportionate, atypical or rapidly progressive.
management: If asthma is present or strongly suspected, include inhaled corticosteroid therapy and avoid LABA monotherapy.
Add long-acting bronchodilator therapy according to persistent symptoms/exacerbation burden and current CTS asthma/COPD guidance.
Address smoking cessation, vaccination, pulmonary rehabilitation/activity and individualized action planning.
medicationSafety: Higher corticosteroid exposure increases candidiasis, dysphonia, bruising and pneumonia/systemic risks; use the minimum effective anti-inflammatory regimen while maintaining asthma safety.
Confirm inhaler technique before escalating multiple devices/classes.
counselling: Teach inhaler technique, adherence and individualized action planning; explain why asthma features make steroid-containing therapy important even when COPD is also present.
followUp: Reassess symptoms, exacerbations, spirometry when useful, smoking status and adverse effects; refer diagnostically complex or treatment-refractory disease.
examTrap: Using LABA bronchodilator monotherapy because the patient has COPD features despite a convincing asthma diagnosis.
oneLinePearl: When asthma is truly part of the picture, protect against asthma risk first—then optimize COPD bronchodilation.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society 2023 Stable COPD Pharmacotherapy Guideline (current)
